claims.text: The starting material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Adding approximately 1–2 at.% Ti will promote Ti segregation to grain boundaries and defect sinks.
Ti-induced stabilization will suppress radiation-induced precipitation.
Ti at grain boundaries and defect sinks will enhance vacancy–interstitial recombination.
Ti addition will kinetically slow solute diffusion.
Ti addition will facilitate grain coarsening during bulk fabrication.
The Ti-modified alloy will retain similarly negligible irradiation hardening at approximately 8 dpa.
Ti atoms preferentially segregate to high-energy sites including grain boundaries, dislocations, and radiation-induced defect clusters.
Segregated Ti traps both vacancies and interstitials.
Reduced solute mobility will inhibit nucleation of radiation-induced precipitates.
A modest Ti addition and possible grain coarsening will improve bulk fabricability without compromising resistance to irradiation-induced hardening.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the Ti-doped alloy will exhibit significantly less radiation-induced precipitation.
The Ti-doped alloy will have improved structural homogeneity conducive to bulk fabrication.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits measurable radiation-induced precipitation after similar irradiation to approximately 8 dpa.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits low irradiation hardening after similar irradiation to approximately 8 dpa.
The proposed behavior applies from 650°C to 1000°C at approximately 8 dpa, where diffusion is active and grain-boundary stabilization remains effective.

contradictions.description: Ti is said to stabilize grain boundaries while also facilitating grain coarsening. Grain-boundary stabilization normally implies resistance to boundary migration and coarsening, and no explanation is provided for reconciling these effects.
